title: Food Preservation & Storage
subtitle: Keep food safe for longer at home and in a small shop by drying, salting, smoking, fermenting, pickling, making jam, and using cold and dry storage the right way.
description: A practical course in household and small-shop food preservation for Nigerian kitchens. You will learn why food spoils, the WHO Five Keys and botulism rules, and then practise drying, salting, smoking, fermenting, pickling and jam making, before mastering fridge and freezer use through power cuts, stock rotation and honest pricing.

Apply the WHO Five Keys and avoid botulism risks from low-acid foods sealed in jars or under oil
Dry, salt and hot-smoke foods and measure your own yields and costs
Make ogi, a vinegar pickle and a jam that keep safely
Run a fridge, freezer and dry store with FEFO rotation and a power-cut plan
Pack, label and price a preserved product from its full cost

modules.title: Why Food Spoils and How to Keep It Safe
modules.overview: Understand the five causes of spoilage, choose the right preservation method for each food, and learn the WHO Five Keys and botulism rules that make every later method safe.

lessons.title: What spoils food in your kitchen: microbes, enzymes, air and pests
objectives: Name the five main causes of food spoilage and give a kitchen example of each
Explain what microbes need to grow and how each preservation method takes one need away
Recognise the early spoilage signs in fresh produce, fish, meat, grains and oils
Sort a market purchase so that damaged items are used or preserved first

blocks.text: Food does not go bad by magic. Every spoiled tomato, sour pot of stew or weevil-filled bag of beans has a cause you can name. When you know the cause, you can choose a method that stops it. This first lesson gives you that understanding, so every later lesson makes sense.

blocks.name: microbe
blocks.caption: Most fast spoilage at home is caused by tiny living things you cannot see: bacteria, yeasts and moulds.

blocks.text: Five causes of spoilage

items: **Microbes.** Bacteria, yeasts and moulds are tiny living things on hands, surfaces, water, soil and the food itself. They feed on food and multiply. Some only change taste and smell. Others, such as the bacteria behind food poisoning, can make people ill without changing how the food looks.

**Enzymes.** These are natural substances inside food that keep working after harvest or slaughter. They make a cut yam or apple turn brown, a banana go soft and black, and vegetables lose colour in a freezer if they were not blanched first.

**Air (oxygen).** Air slowly reacts with fats and oils. That is why groundnuts, crayfish, palm oil and fried snacks can develop a sharp, stale smell called rancidity. Air also lets moulds grow on the surface of food.
**Pests.** Weevils, beetles, moths, cockroaches, ants, rats and lizards eat food and leave droppings, hairs and eggs that carry germs.

**Physical damage.** Bruises, cracks and cuts break the natural skin of fruit, vegetables, eggs and grains. Microbes and air enter through the wound, and the item spoils days earlier than its neighbours.

blocks.text: What microbes need

Microbes need the same few things almost all the time: **food, water, warmth, time** and, for most of them, **air**. Take one away and they slow down or stop. This is the idea behind every method in this course. Drying and salting take away water. Refrigeration and freezing take away warmth. Pickling and fermenting make the food too sour (acidic) for harmful bacteria. Sugar in jam ties up water. Sealing takes away air, but be careful: one dangerous bacterium, *Clostridium botulinum*, grows only where there is **no** air, so sealing alone can make some foods more dangerous, not less. Lesson 3 explains this in detail.

Warmth matters a lot in Nigeria. The World Health Organization (WHO) Five Keys to Safer Food poster marks the range between **5°C and 60°C** as the danger zone, where bacteria multiply quickly. A kitchen afternoon in most Nigerian towns sits inside that zone. That is why cooked rice left on the stove overnight, or fish left in a bowl after market, can become unsafe even when it smells fine.

blocks.title: Worked example: sorting a basket of tomatoes
blocks.context: For example, Bisi buys a basket of 60 tomatoes for about ₦18,000 (an approximate price; market prices change weekly). On the bus home some get squeezed.
steps: She tips the basket gently onto a clean tray, never leaving the tomatoes packed tight in the heat.
She finds 9 tomatoes with soft or split skin. That is 9 ÷ 60 = 15% of the basket.
Each tomato cost her about ₦18,000 ÷ 60 = ₦300, so the damaged ones are worth about 9 × ₦300 = ₦2,700.
She washes and blends the 9 damaged tomatoes that same evening for stew, and spreads the other 51 in a single layer in a cool, airy spot.
She checks the tray every morning and moves any newly softening tomato into the cooking pile.
blocks.result: Instead of losing ₦2,700 of tomatoes, plus the healthy ones they would have infected, Bisi uses the damaged ones at once and keeps the rest good for several more days.

blocks.title: Buy for your storage, not for the bargain
blocks.text: A big basket is cheaper per tomato only if you can use or preserve it before it spoils. If your space and time allow you to handle only half a basket, buying half is often the cheaper choice.

Notice that smell and appearance are useful early signs of **spoilage**, but they are not proof of **safety**. Many food poisoning bacteria grow without any change you can see or smell. So the rules in this course are about preventing growth in the first place: clean hands and surfaces, the right temperature, the right amount of salt, acid or sugar, and the right storage time.

takeaways: Spoilage has five main causes: microbes, enzymes, air, pests and physical damage.
Microbes need food, water, warmth, time and usually air; every method removes at least one.
WHO marks 5°C to 60°C as the danger zone where bacteria grow quickly.
Remove damaged items early, because one bruise can spoil a whole basket.
Food that looks and smells fine can still be unsafe.

activity.title: Spoilage walk in your own kitchen
steps: Walk through your kitchen and store with a notebook or your phone notes app.
Find three foods showing early spoilage signs and write which of the five causes is at work in each.
For each one, write the 'need' you could take away (water, warmth, air or time) to slow it down.
Sort one basket or bag of produce, separating damaged items from sound ones, and use or preserve the damaged ones today.
activity.evidence: A short note or voice note listing three spoiled foods, their cause, and what you changed, plus a photo of your sorted produce.

lessons.title: Matching each food to a preservation method
objectives: Describe how drying, salting, smoking, fermenting, pickling, sugar preserving, cooling and freezing each stop spoilage
Choose a suitable method for a given food, budget and level of power supply
Explain the hurdle idea of combining two or more mild methods
Plan the order of work when several foods need preserving at once

blocks.text: There is no single best method. A good preserver looks at the food, the equipment and power she has, how long she needs it to keep, and whether she will eat it or sell it. Then she picks a method, or a combination of methods. This lesson gives you a map of the main options so you can make that choice quickly.

blocks.text: The hurdle idea

Food scientists talk about **hurdles**. Each method is a hurdle a microbe has to jump. One very high hurdle, like hard freezing, can be enough on its own. But several smaller hurdles together are often safer and give better taste. Smoked fish, for example, is salted (hurdle one), partly dried by the heat (hurdle two), coated with smoke (hurdle three), and then stored in a dry, airy place (hurdle four). Pepper sauce is cooked (one), acidified with vinegar (two), packed hot into clean jars (three) and refrigerated after opening (four).

blocks.text: Questions to ask before you choose

items: **What is the food?** Acidic foods such as most fruit behave very differently from low-acid foods such as fish, meat, beans and most vegetables.
**How long must it keep?** Two days for a party, two weeks for the family, or six months for sale?
**What equipment and power do you have?** A freezer is only as good as your electricity or generator hours. Sun, salt, vinegar and sugar work without power.
**Will you sell it?** Food for sale must be consistent, labelled and, for packaged products, registered with NAFDAC. Start with methods you can repeat exactly.
**What does your household or customer like?** Preserved food that nobody eats is still waste.

blocks.title: Worked example: one weekend, three surplus foods
blocks.context: For example, Halima comes home from her cousin's farm with 6 kg of ripe mango, 3 kg of fresh tilapia and a large bundle of ugwu. She has one empty freezer shelf, two mesh drying trays and about 6 hours of power a day.
steps: Fish spoils fastest, so she deals with it first. She guts and cleans it, divides it into 500 g packs, which gives 3,000 g ÷ 500 g = 6 packs, labels them and freezes them flat so they freeze quickly.
Ugwu wilts within a day or two. She blanches it, squeezes out water and freezes it in 4 small soup-sized bags on the same shelf.
Mango keeps a few days if it is not bruised. Each tray holds about 1.5 kg of slices, so 6 kg needs 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4 tray-loads. With 2 trays she needs 2 sunny days.
She eats or shares the softest mangoes now instead of drying them, because bruised fruit dries poorly.
blocks.result: Everything is protected within two days, the freezer is used only for the foods that need it, and the free sun does the work for the mango.

blocks.title: Preserving does not repair spoiled food
blocks.text: Every method only slows or stops future spoilage. It cannot make bad food good again. Drying a mouldy tomato or smoking a fish that already smells gives you a spoiled product that lasts longer. Start with fresh, sound food every time.

In the next lesson you will learn the safety rules that apply to all of these methods. In Modules 2 to 4 you will practise the methods one by one, always with a worked example and a test you can do at home.

takeaways: Choose a method by the food, how long it must keep, your equipment and power, and whether you will sell it.
Low-acid foods (fish, meat, beans, most vegetables) need more care than acidic fruit.
Several mild hurdles together often work better than one.
Deal with the fastest-spoiling food first.
Preservation never fixes food that has already started to spoil.

activity.title: Your household preservation map
steps: List five foods your household often wastes or buys in bulk.
For each, note whether it is acidic or low-acid, and how long you need it to keep.
Choose a main method and one extra hurdle for each, using the table in this lesson.
Mark which methods need power and which do not, and circle the one you will practise first.

lessons.title: Safe preserving: WHO Five Keys, botulism and when to throw food out
objectives: Apply the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food to home preserving
Explain why low-acid foods sealed in jars or covered in oil can carry botulism
Identify the danger signs that mean a preserved food must be thrown away
Decide safely what to do with a risky product idea

blocks.text: Preserving gives food a long life. That is good for your pocket, but it also gives any harmful microbe a long time to grow if the process was wrong. This lesson sets the safety rules for the rest of the course. Read it carefully, and come back to it whenever you try a new recipe.

blocks.name: warning-sign
blocks.caption: A few clear safety rules protect your family and your customers from the rare but serious dangers of preserved food.

blocks.text: The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
The World Health Organization teaches five simple keys. They apply to preserving just as much as to cooking.

blocks.title: WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
items: Keep clean
Separate raw and cooked
Cook thoroughly
Keep food at safe temperatures
Use safe water and raw materials
blocks.caption: Check all five keys before you start any preserving job.

items: **Keep clean.** Wash your hands before handling food and often during preparation, and after using the toilet. Wash and sanitise surfaces and equipment. Protect food and kitchen areas from insects, pests and other animals.

**Separate raw and cooked.** Keep raw meat, poultry and seafood away from other foods. Use separate knives and boards for raw foods, and store foods in containers so raw and prepared foods do not touch.
**Cook thoroughly.** Bring soups and stews to the boil so they reach 70°C. Reheat cooked food thoroughly.

**Keep food at safe temperatures.** Do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours. Refrigerate cooked and perishable food promptly, preferably below 5°C. Keep hot food above 60°C. Do not store food too long even in the fridge, and do not thaw frozen food at room temperature.
**Use safe water and raw materials.** Use safe or treated water. Choose fresh, wholesome food, wash fruit and vegetables, and do not use food beyond its expiry date.

blocks.text: Botulism: the hidden danger in sealed jars and oil

Botulism is a rare but very serious illness caused by a toxin from the bacterium *Clostridium botulinum*. WHO explains that this bacterium can only grow **without oxygen**, and it **will not grow in acidic conditions (pH below 4.6)**. Its spores survive ordinary boiling. WHO names **home-made canned, preserved or fermented foods** as a common source, including low-acid preserved vegetables, and fish that has been fermented, salted or smoked.

Think about what that means in a Nigerian kitchen. A sealed jar, a tightly tied nylon bag or a layer of oil on top of food all shut out air. If the food under the seal is **low-acid** (vegetables, garlic, ginger, onions, pepper paste without vinegar, beans, fish, meat) and it sits at room temperature, the conditions suit this bacterium. The food may look, smell and taste normal.

blocks.title: Low-acid foods in oil or sealed jars
blocks.text: Never store raw or cooked garlic, ginger, onions, herbs, vegetables, pepper paste, fish or meat under oil, or in a sealed jar, at room temperature unless you are following a tested recipe that makes it acidic or uses proper pressure canning. Oil on top does not preserve food; it removes air and can help botulism bacteria grow. Make oil-based mixtures in small amounts, keep them in the fridge, and use them up quickly. Do not sell home-made garlic or ginger in oil.

WHO notes that symptoms usually begin 12 to 36 hours after eating (sometimes 4 hours to 8 days) with marked tiredness, weakness and dizziness, followed by blurred vision, dry mouth and difficulty swallowing and speaking. It can paralyse the muscles used for breathing. Anyone with these signs after eating preserved food needs a hospital at once. WHO also states that the toxin is destroyed by boiling (for example, an internal temperature above 85°C for 5 minutes or longer), but this does not make it acceptable to eat a suspicious jar: throw it away.

blocks.title: Honey and babies
blocks.text: WHO warns parents and caregivers not to feed honey to babies under 1 year old, because honey can carry botulism spores.
Signs that mean: throw it away

head: Sign
What it means
rows: Lid bulging, or liquid spurts out when opened
Gas made by microbes inside the jar
Mould on jam, pickles, ogi or dried food
Mould roots go deeper than you can see; do not scrape and eat
Unexpected cloudiness, bubbles or slime in a pickle that was clear
Unwanted microbes are growing
Off, rotten or unusual smell
Spoilage; never taste to check
Mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured groundnuts or maize
Possible aflatoxin, a mould poison WHO links to maize and groundnuts

blocks.text: When you throw away a suspicious jar, do not open it near food. Wrap it in a bag and put it in a covered bin away from children and animals, then wash your hands and the surface.

blocks.title: Worked example: a risky product idea
blocks.context: For example, Amaka runs a small provisions shop in Enugu. Customers ask for ready-made blended garlic and ginger in oil, and she plans to make 20 jars a week to sell from the shelf.
steps: She checks the food: garlic and ginger are low-acid. That is one warning.
She checks the packing: a layer of oil and a sealed lid shut out air. That is a second warning.
She checks the storage: her shelf is at room temperature for weeks. That is a third warning.
Three warnings together match the conditions WHO describes for botulism, so she drops the idea.
Instead she sells sun-dried ginger slices and a vinegar-based pepper sauce made from a tested recipe, which are safer at room temperature.
blocks.result: Amaka protects her customers and her shop's name, and still meets the demand with two safer products.

blocks.text: Safety rules can feel strict, but they are what allow you to preserve with confidence. If you are ever unsure, keep the food cold, use it quickly, or throw it out.

takeaways: The WHO Five Keys apply to every preserving job.
Botulism bacteria grow without air and not below pH 4.6, so low-acid foods sealed in jars or under oil are the risk.
Oil on top does not preserve food.
Bulging lids, mould, slime, unexpected cloudiness and off smells mean throw it away, without tasting.
Never give honey to a baby under 1 year.

activity.title: Safety audit of your preserved foods
steps: Collect every home-made jar, bottle and bag of preserved food in your house.
For each, write whether it is acidic or low-acid and how it is stored (open, sealed, under oil, fridge).
Mark any low-acid food sealed or under oil at room temperature, and move it to the fridge or throw it away.
Check every item for the danger signs in the table and discard any that show them, safely wrapped.
Stick a printed or handwritten copy of the Five Keys near your preparation area.
activity.evidence: A list of your preserved foods with the decision for each, and a photo of the Five Keys posted in your kitchen.

quiz.q: Ngozi leaves cooked jollof rice on the stove from 9 pm until 7 am. According to the WHO Five Keys, what is the problem?
options: Cooked food should not stay at room temperature more than 2 hours
Rice must be kept above 85°C all night
Nothing, if the pot lid is closed
quiz.explain: WHO advises not to leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours; the night kitchen is inside the 5°C to 60°C danger zone.

quiz.q: Which of these is the riskiest product to keep on a shop shelf at room temperature?
options: Hard, brittle dried tomato flakes in a sealed bag
Unopened guava jam made with plenty of sugar
Blended raw garlic covered with oil in a sealed jar
Vinegar-pickled onions from a tested recipe
quiz.explain: Garlic is low-acid and the oil and lid shut out air, the conditions where botulism bacteria can grow.

quiz.q: Drying tomatoes mainly stops spoilage by taking away which need of microbes?
quiz.explain: Drying removes water. Without enough water, bacteria and moulds cannot multiply.

quiz.q: A jar of home-made pepper sauce has a domed lid and fizzes when opened, but smells fine. What should you do?
options: Boil it and use it at once
Wrap it and throw it away without tasting
Scoop off the top and refrigerate the rest
quiz.explain: A bulging lid and fizzing mean microbes made gas inside. Never taste to check; throw it away safely.

quiz.q: Smoked fish is first salted, then hot-smoked, then kept in a dry airy basket. This is an example of:
options: The hurdle idea: several methods together
quiz.explain: Salt, heat drying, smoke and dry storage are separate hurdles that together keep the fish.

quiz.q: Halima has fresh fish, ripe mango and ugwu but limited freezer space. Which should she handle first?
options: The mango, because it is sweetest
The ugwu, because it is lightest
The fish, because it spoils fastest
All three can wait a week
quiz.explain: Fresh fish spoils fastest in the heat, so it goes into the freezer or into processing first.

modules.overview: Use sun, salt and smoke, the three oldest African preservation methods, cleanly and safely: dry vegetables and fruit, salt and dry fish, and hot-smoke fish with yields and costs you have measured yourself.

lessons.title: Drying tomatoes, leafy vegetables and mango at home
objectives: Prepare tomatoes, leafy vegetables and mango correctly for drying
Dry food hygienically in the sun or in a simple solar dryer
Test dryness by touch and by a one-week jar check (conditioning)
Calculate drying yield and the cost of 100 g of dried product

blocks.text: Drying is the cheapest preservation method in a sunny country. It needs no electricity, and dried food is light, so it takes little space. But careless drying gives dusty, mouldy food that spoils in weeks. This lesson shows you how to dry three very different foods well: tomatoes (juicy and acidic), leafy vegetables (thin and delicate) and mango (sweet and fleshy).

blocks.name: tomato
blocks.caption: Tomatoes are the classic drying crop: cheap and plentiful in the glut season, costly in the scarce months.

blocks.text: Rules for every drying job

items: **Raised and covered.** Dry food on mesh or woven trays raised off the ground, never on a mat or zinc sheet on the floor. Cover with clean net or mosquito mesh to keep off flies, birds, dust and lizards.
**Air above and below.** Mesh lets air pass under the food, so it dries on both sides at once.
**Single layer, even size.** Pieces should not touch. Cut everything to about the same thickness so it all dries at the same rate.
**Bring it in at night.** Night air is damp and food left out takes back water. Bring trays inside, covered, and put them out again in the morning.
**Clean hands, clean water.** Wash produce in safe water and wash your hands and knives before cutting.

blocks.text: A simple solar dryer

A solar dryer is a box or tent with a clear plastic or glass cover, a dark surface inside to absorb heat, and air vents low on one side and high on the other. Warm air rises through the food and leaves through the top vent, carrying water away. It dries faster than open sun, protects food from rain and insects, and keeps colour better. You can build one from wood, mesh and clear polythene. Keep the vents covered with net so insects cannot enter.

blocks.title: Drying from fresh to stored
items: Select firm, sound produce
Wash, cut evenly, pre-treat
Dry raised and covered
Test dryness and condition
Pack airtight, store cool
blocks.caption: Each step removes a chance for mould or insects to spoil the batch.

blocks.text: Preparing each food

head: Food
Preparation
Dry when
rows: Tomatoes
Choose firm, ripe, unbruised fruit. Wash, cut into even slices or halves, remove the hard stem end. A light sprinkle of salt is optional for taste
Leathery to brittle, no wet centre, no juice when you press or fold a piece
Leafy vegetables (ugwu, spinach, bitter leaf, moringa)
Strip leaves from thick stems, wash well. Dip briefly in boiling water just until they turn bright green and wilt, drain and spread thinly. This blanching helps keep the green colour
Leaves crumble when rubbed between your fingers
Mango
Choose ripe but firm fruit. Peel, cut into thin even slices about half a centimetre thick. A quick dip in water with lemon or lime juice reduces browning
Leathery and bendy, with no sticky wet spots when you tear a piece

blocks.title: Turn and check daily
blocks.text: Turn pieces once or twice a day. Remove any piece that turns mouldy, dark and soft, or crawling with insects, so it does not spread to the rest.
Is it dry enough? The conditioning check

Pieces on the edge of a tray dry faster than those in the middle, so some may still hold water when the batch feels dry. Before you pack for long storage, **condition** the batch: fill a clean, dry glass jar about two-thirds full, close it and shake it once a day for about a week. If drops of water form inside the jar, or pieces stick together, spread the food out and dry it more. If it stays loose and dry, it is ready to pack.

blocks.title: Worked example: tomato yield and cost
blocks.context: For example, Funmi in Kaduna buys 4 kg of tomatoes at about ₦1,200 per kg in the glut season (an approximate price; check your own market) and dries them on two solar dryer trays.
steps: After drying and conditioning she weighs the batch on a kitchen scale: 400 g of dried tomato.
Her drying ratio is 4,000 g ÷ 400 g = 10, so 10 kg of fresh tomato gives about 1 kg dried in her dryer.
400 g makes 4 packs of 100 g, so the tomato cost per 100 g pack is ₦4,800 ÷ 4 = ₦1,200, before bags, labels and her time.
She records the ratio in her notebook so next time she knows that 1 kg of dried tomato needs about 10 kg fresh.
blocks.result: Funmi now knows her real yield and the minimum value of each 100 g pack. Yield changes with the variety, ripeness and how dry you go, so always weigh your own batch.

blocks.text: Packing and storing dried food

items: Let food cool fully before packing; warm food sweats inside the bag.
Pack in clean, dry, airtight containers: glass jars with good lids, thick food-grade zip bags, or heat-sealed bags.
Pack in small amounts so each opening exposes only a little food to damp air.
Store in a cool, dark, dry place away from the stove, the sink and the outside wall that gets the sun.
Check every week for moisture, mould or insects, and use the oldest pack first.

blocks.title: Dried tomatoes in oil
blocks.text: Packing dried tomatoes under oil turns a safe dry food into a low-oxygen food. Keep oil-packed tomatoes in the fridge, make small amounts and use them quickly, as you learned in Lesson 3.

takeaways: Dry on raised, covered mesh, in a single even layer, and bring trays in at night.
A solar dryer is faster and cleaner than open sun.
Blanch leafy vegetables briefly and treat mango with lemon water to keep colour.
Condition the batch in a jar for about a week before long storage.
Weigh fresh and dried food to know your real yield and cost.

activity.title: Dry and condition one batch
steps: Choose 1 to 2 kg of tomatoes, mango or leafy vegetables and weigh them.
Prepare and dry them on a raised, covered tray, bringing them in each night.
Weigh the dried batch and calculate your drying ratio.
Condition the batch in a jar for a week, recording each day whether you see moisture.
Pack the dried food in small labelled packs with the date.
activity.evidence: Photos of the tray and finished packs, plus a note of fresh weight, dry weight, drying ratio and conditioning results.

lessons.title: Salting fish and meat: dry salting, brining and drying
objectives: Explain how salt preserves fish and meat and why salting alone is not enough
Carry out dry salting and brining hygienically
Finish salted fish by drying and store it safely
Work out the true cost per kilogram of a salted product

blocks.text: Salt has preserved fish and meat for thousands of years. Salt pulls water out of the flesh and leaves too little free water for most spoilage bacteria. It also firms the flesh and adds flavour. But salt works slowly from the outside in, and WHO lists salted fish among the foods that can carry botulism when the process goes wrong. So salting is always done with care, and almost always followed by drying, smoking or cold storage.

blocks.name: salt-shaker
blocks.caption: Salt draws water out of fish and meat, the first hurdle against spoilage.

blocks.text: Two ways to salt

head: Point
Dry salting
Brining (wet salting)
rows: How
Rub salt into the flesh and pack fish in layers with salt between them
Soak fish in a strong salt solution
Result
Firmer, saltier, drier product that keeps longer
Milder, more even salt; good before smoking
Best for
Fish you will store dry for weeks
Fish you will smoke, or eat within days
Watch
Every surface, including the belly cavity, must touch salt
Fish must stay fully under the brine; keep it cool and covered

blocks.text: Step by step: dry-salted fish

items: Start with very fresh fish. Bright clear eyes, red gills, firm flesh and a clean sea or river smell. Salting will not rescue fish that is already stale.
Gut the fish, remove the gills and wash the belly cavity well with safe water. The gut is the part that spoils fastest.
Split thick fish open along the back or belly, or cut deep slashes, so salt can reach the thickest part.
Use clean, dry food-grade salt. Rub it into every surface and fill the belly cavity.
Layer fish and salt in a clean plastic or food-grade container, skin side down, with salt between each layer and a thick layer on top. Cover and keep it in the coolest shaded place you have.
Liquid (pickle) will collect as salt draws water out. Drain it as your tested family or extension recipe directs.
Rinse off loose salt and dry the fish on raised, covered racks in the sun or a solar dryer, bringing it in at night, until it is firm and dry right through.

blocks.title: Making a full-strength brine
blocks.text: To make a strong brine without measuring tools, stir salt into clean water until no more dissolves and some salt stays at the bottom. A saturated brine like this is as salty as plain water can get, so the strength is the same every time.

blocks.title: From fresh fish to stored salted fish
items: Gut, wash, split
Salt every surface
Drain the pickle
Dry on raised racks
Store dry and cool
blocks.caption: Salt starts the work; drying and dry storage finish it.

blocks.text: How do you know the salting worked? Well salted and dried fish is firm, pale or golden, and smells clean and salty. The flesh near the bone is as firm as the outside. Warning signs are a soft, wet or pink centre, a sour or rotten smell when you press the thickest part, or slime on the surface. Fish with these signs is not safe to store and should be thrown away, not re-salted.
Salting meat

Meat is salted in a similar way, but it must be cut into thin strips first so salt and heat reach the centre quickly. Northern Nigerian **kilishi** is a familiar example: thin sheets of beef dried, coated with spiced groundnut paste, dried again and roasted. If you salt and dry meat at home, cut it thin, keep it covered from flies, dry it fully, and cook it thoroughly before eating.

blocks.title: Worked example: true cost of salted fish
blocks.context: For example, Chioma in Calabar buys 5 kg of fresh croaker at about ₦3,000 per kg and 2 kg of salt at about ₦800 per kg (approximate prices).
steps: Fish cost: 5 × ₦3,000 = ₦15,000. Salt cost: 2 × ₦800 = ₦1,600. Total ingredients: ₦16,600.
After gutting and removing gills, the fish weighs 4.2 kg.
After salting and drying, she weighs the finished fish: 2.5 kg.
Cost per kilogram of finished fish: ₦16,600 ÷ 2.5 = ₦6,640, before packaging and her time.
Finished weight as a share of what she bought: 2.5 ÷ 5 = 50%.
blocks.result: Chioma sees that each kilogram of salted fish cost her ₦6,640 in ingredients alone, more than twice the fresh price per kilogram, so she prices from that figure, not from the fresh price.

blocks.text: Storing and using salted fish

items: Store fully dried salted fish in a clean, airy basket or carton, off the floor, away from damp walls and covered against flies.
Keep partly dried or lightly salted fish in the fridge and use it within days.
Check weekly for mould, soft wet patches, a rotten smell or insect damage; discard any affected pieces.
Before cooking, soak salted fish in clean water, changing the water several times, to remove excess salt.

blocks.title: Lightly salted fish at room temperature
blocks.text: Lightly salted fish that is not dried, smoked or kept cold is not preserved. Do not seal it in a bag or jar at room temperature. Either dry it fully, smoke it, or refrigerate it and cook it soon.

takeaways: Salt pulls water out of flesh, but works slowly from the outside in.
Use only very fresh fish; gut it, wash it and split thick fish.
Dry salting gives a longer-keeping product; brining gives milder fish for smoking.
Salting must be followed by drying, smoking or refrigeration.
Calculate cost per kilogram of finished product, not fresh weight.

activity.title: Salt and dry a small batch of fish
steps: Buy 1 to 2 kg of very fresh small fish and weigh it.
Gut, wash and split the fish, then dry-salt it in a covered container.
Drain, rinse and dry it on raised covered racks until firm right through.
Weigh the finished fish and calculate your cost per kilogram.
Store it in an airy, covered container and record its condition each week for a month.
activity.evidence: Photos of each stage, the weights, your cost per kilogram and your four weekly storage notes.

lessons.title: Hot-smoking fish safely in a drum or kiln
objectives: Prepare fish for hot-smoking so it cooks and dries evenly
Run a smoking session that cooks the fish without burning it
Protect yourself and others from smoke and fire
Store smoked fish and calculate yield and cost per kilogram

blocks.text: Smoked fish is part of almost every Nigerian kitchen, from stockfish-style dried catfish to smoked mackerel and bonga. Hot-smoking does three jobs together: the heat cooks the fish, the warm air dries it, and the smoke leaves a coating that adds flavour and helps slow surface mould. Done well, hard-smoked fish keeps for weeks in a dry place. Done badly, it is burnt outside, wet inside, and spoils quickly.

blocks.name: fish
blocks.caption: Small and medium fish such as catfish, mackerel and bonga are commonly hot-smoked in West Africa.

blocks.text: Soft-smoked or hard-smoked

head: Point
Soft-smoked (short smoke)
Hard-smoked (long smoke and dry)
rows: Texture
Moist and tender
Dry and firm, sometimes brittle
Keeps
A short time; treat like cooked fish
Weeks if kept dry and pest-free
Store
Refrigerate and eat within days, or re-smoke
Airy basket or carton in a dry place
Used for
Eating soon, pepper soup, sale the same day
Soups and stews, trading to other towns

blocks.text: Preparing the fish

items: Use only fresh fish. Smoking does not repair stale fish.
Gut the fish and remove gills. Wash in safe water. For catfish, scrub off the slime.
For thick fish, make deep cuts across the body so heat and smoke reach the bone.
Brine the fish in a full-strength salt solution, or rub with salt, for flavour and to firm the surface. Drain well.
Arrange fish on clean wire racks in one layer, not touching, so smoke and air can circulate.

blocks.text: Running the smoke

Hot-smoking is a slow process with three stages. First, gentle heat and good airflow dry the wet surface. Next, higher heat cooks the fish through: the flesh should turn opaque and come away firmly from the bone. Last, low heat over many hours drives out water for long keeping. Turn and rotate racks so fish near the fire does not burn while the top rack stays wet.

How do you check that the fish is cooked and dry? Break open the thickest fish on the lowest-heat part of the rack. Cooked flesh is opaque all the way to the bone, with no pink, glassy or watery parts. Hard-smoked fish should feel light for its size, firm when pressed, and sound dry when two fish are tapped together. If the centre still feels soft and damp, the fish needs more time on low heat, not more fire.

blocks.title: A hot-smoking session
items: Clean, salt and drain
Gentle heat dries surface
Hotter heat cooks through
Low heat dries for keeping
Cool, then store dry
blocks.caption: Moving through the stages slowly cooks and dries the fish without burning it.

items: Use dry, untreated hardwood, coconut husk or charcoal. **Never** burn plastic, tyres, painted, varnished or chemically treated wood: they release poisonous smoke that settles on the food.
Keep fish well above the flames. Fat dripping into an open flame flares up and blackens fish, and burnt, charred fish carries more harmful smoke substances.
Aim for a steady smoulder, not a blaze. Control heat by adding or removing fuel and opening or closing vents.

blocks.title: Protect your lungs, eyes and family
blocks.text: Wood smoke harms the lungs and eyes, especially when you work beside it for many hours every week. Smoke outdoors or under an open shed, with your back to the wind, never inside a closed kitchen or bedroom. Use a smoker or kiln with a chimney that carries smoke up and away from your face. Keep children and babies away from the smoking area, keep water or sand nearby for fire, and wear cotton clothes, not synthetic fabric that melts.

blocks.title: Worked example: yield and cost of smoked catfish
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat in Lokoja buys 10 kg of live catfish at about ₦3,500 per kg, and uses about ₦4,000 of firewood and ₦500 of salt (approximate prices).
steps: After a full hard-smoke she weighs the finished fish: 3.5 kg.
Yield: 3.5 ÷ 10 = 35% of the fresh weight.
Cost per kilogram of smoked catfish: ₦39,500 ÷ 3.5 = about ₦11,286.
She notes that a soft smoke would leave more weight but would need refrigeration and quick sale.
blocks.result: Rukayat knows that each kilogram of her hard-smoked catfish costs about ₦11,300 before packaging and labour, and that she loses about two-thirds of the weight as water.

blocks.text: Storing smoked fish

items: Let fish cool completely before packing, or it will sweat and grow mould.
Store hard-smoked fish in clean cartons, baskets or paper, in a dry, airy place off the floor. Do not seal it in plastic while it is still warm.
Check weekly. If you find damp patches or beginning mould, or small beetles and larvae, remove affected fish. Lightly re-smoking or re-drying sound fish restores dryness.

Throw away fish that smells rotten, feels slimy, or has mould deep in the flesh. WHO lists smoked fish among foods linked to botulism when badly processed, so never seal soft-smoked fish airtight at room temperature.

takeaways: Hot-smoking cooks, dries and coats the fish in one process.
Soft-smoked fish is perishable; only hard-smoked fish keeps for weeks.
Use clean dry wood or charcoal, never plastic, tyres or treated wood, and avoid charring.
Smoke outdoors with a chimney and keep children away.
Weigh before and after to know your yield and real cost per kilogram.

activity.title: Plan and record a smoking session
steps: Draw your smoker or kiln and mark where smoke leaves and where you will stand.
Smoke at least 2 kg of fish through all three stages, turning racks regularly.
Record start and end times, fuel used, and fresh and smoked weights.
Calculate yield and cost per kilogram.
Store the fish and check it weekly for a month, noting its condition.
activity.evidence: A smoking record sheet with weights, times, fuel cost, yield and cost per kilogram, plus photos of the setup and finished fish.

quiz.q: Funmi dries 6 kg of fresh tomatoes and gets 600 g of dried tomato. What is her drying ratio?
quiz.explain: 6,000 g ÷ 600 g = 10, so 10 kg of fresh tomato gives about 1 kg dried.

quiz.q: After a week in a closed jar, drops of water appear on the inside of the glass holding Funmi's dried mango. What should she do?
options: Pack it for sale at once
Spread it out and dry it more
Put it in the freezer for an hour
quiz.explain: Moisture during conditioning means some pieces are not dry enough. More drying prevents mould.

quiz.q: Why are drying trays raised and covered with net?
options: So air reaches both sides and flies, dust and animals stay off
To stop the sun reaching the food
quiz.explain: Raised mesh lets air dry both sides; netting protects against insects, birds and dust.

quiz.q: Which fuel is safe to use in a fish smoker?
quiz.explain: Tyres, plastics and painted or treated wood give off poisonous smoke that settles on the fish.

quiz.q: Rukayat smokes 8 kg of fresh fish and ends with 2.8 kg. What is her yield?
quiz.explain: 2.8 ÷ 8 = 0.35, so 35% of the fresh weight remains.

options: Seal it in a jar on the shelf
Keep it in the fridge and cook it soon, or dry it fully
Leave it in the salting liquid on the counter for a month
quiz.explain: Lightly salted fish is not preserved. It must be dried, smoked or refrigerated and used quickly.

modules.title: Fermenting, Pickling and Jam Making
modules.overview: Use acid and sugar to preserve: make and keep ogi and fermented vegetables, pack vinegar pickles and pepper sauces without weakening the acid, and make jam that sets and keeps.

lessons.title: Ogi and fermented vegetables: controlled souring at home
objectives: Explain how fermentation preserves food by making it sour
Make and keep ogi (akamu) hygienically
Keep fermenting vegetables under brine and judge a good ferment from a spoiled one
Cost a batch of ogi and price it by portion

blocks.text: Fermentation is one of Africa's oldest food skills. Ogi (akamu), fufu, garri, iru (dawadawa), ogiri and nono are all fermented. In a good ferment, friendly bacteria, mostly lactic acid bacteria, eat some of the sugar in the food and turn it into acid. The food becomes sour, and that sourness makes life hard for many harmful bacteria. You are not killing microbes; you are helping the right ones win.

blocks.name: ear-of-maize
blocks.caption: Maize, sorghum and millet are steeped, milled and soured to make ogi.

blocks.text: The friendly bacteria need a fair start: clean grain or vegetables, safe water, clean containers and the right amount of time. If the start is dirty, or the water is unsafe, unwanted microbes can win instead. That is why the WHO key **use safe water and raw materials** matters so much here: ogi is made almost entirely of water.
Making ogi step by step

items: **Clean the grain.** Pick out stones, shrivelled, discoloured or mouldy grains. Mouldy maize can carry aflatoxin, a mould poison; washing or souring does not remove it.
**Steep.** Cover the grain with plenty of safe water in a clean, covered bucket. Leave it for about one to three days until a grain crushes easily between your fingers.
**Wet-mill.** Drain and grind the soft grain at the mill or with a blender. Some households add ginger, cloves or pepper for flavour.
**Sieve.** Mix the paste with safe water and pass it through a fine sieve or clean cloth, squeezing well. Keep the white liquid; the husk left behind can be used for animal feed.
**Settle and sour.** Cover the white liquid and leave it to settle for about one to three days. It will smell pleasantly sour as the starch sinks to the bottom.
**Pour off the top water.** The thick white sediment is ogi. Keep it as it is, wrap it in leaves or clean food bags, or press out the water to make a firmer cake.

blocks.title: From grain to ogi
items: Clean and steep grain
Wet-mill the soft grain
Sieve with safe water
Settle and sour
Store under fresh water
blocks.caption: Every stage uses safe water and covered, clean containers.

blocks.text: Keeping ogi

items: Keep wet ogi in a covered container with a layer of safe water on top, and change that top water daily. This keeps air off the surface and stops it drying out.
In hot weather it sours further each day. Keep it in the fridge if you have power, and make amounts your household or customers will use within a few days.
Use a clean, dry spoon every time. Never put your hand into the container.
Pap (akamu) is made by stirring ogi with boiling water or cooking it until thick. Prepare it fresh for each meal, especially for children.

head: Good ferment
Spoiled ferment: throw it away
rows: Clean, pleasantly sour smell
Rotten, putrid or strong cheesy smell
White or cream colour
Pink, black, green or orange patches
Smooth paste, clear top water
Slime, fuzzy mould or a thick coloured film
Grain sorted before steeping
Made from mouldy or insect-damaged grain

blocks.text: Fermented vegetables

Shredded cabbage, carrots, cucumber or garden egg can be fermented in salt brine in the same way. The rules: weigh the vegetables and the salt so every batch is the same; follow a tested recipe for the amount of salt; keep every piece **under** the brine with a clean weight such as a small plate or a water-filled food bag; cover the jar loosely so gas can escape; and keep it in the coolest place in the house. A good ferment bubbles gently and smells clean and sour. When it is as sour as you like, move it to the fridge.

blocks.title: Fermented fish and other low-acid ferments
blocks.text: WHO names home-fermented foods, including fermented fish, as a common source of botulism. Ferments that do not become clearly sour, or that are sealed airtight and kept warm, are the risky ones. Do not invent new fermented fish or meat products for sale; stick to known methods and keep them cold.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing ogi by portion
blocks.context: For example, Tolu in Ibadan makes ogi to sell to neighbours. She buys 3 kg of maize at about ₦900 per kg, pays about ₦500 at the mill, and adds about ₦300 of ginger (approximate prices).
steps: She weighs the finished wet ogi after pouring off the top water: 5.4 kg.
She wraps it in 300 g portions: 5,400 g ÷ 300 g = 18 portions.
Cost per portion: ₦3,500 ÷ 18 = about ₦194.
Because ogi keeps only a few days without a fridge, she takes orders on WhatsApp first and makes only what is ordered.
blocks.result: Tolu knows each wrap costs her about ₦194 before her time and leaves, so any price below that loses money, and making to order cuts her waste.

takeaways: Fermentation preserves food by helping friendly bacteria make it sour.
Start with clean, sorted grain and safe water; souring cannot remove aflatoxin from mouldy grain.
Keep ogi under fresh water changed daily, in a covered container, and use it within a few days.
Keep fermenting vegetables under the brine and move them to the fridge once sour.
Pink, black or fuzzy mould, slime or a rotten smell means throw it away.

activity.title: Make and keep one batch of ogi
steps: Sort and weigh 1 kg of maize, sorghum or millet, removing any mouldy grains.
Steep, mill, sieve and settle it, using only safe water and covered containers.
Weigh the finished ogi and calculate the cost per 300 g portion.
Keep it under fresh water, changing the water daily, and note its smell and look each day for five days.
activity.evidence: A short batch record with weights, costs, cost per portion, and five daily observation notes or photos.

lessons.title: Vinegar pickles and pepper sauces that stay safe
objectives: Explain why acid makes pickles safe and why the vinegar must not be weakened
Sterilise jars and pack a refrigerator pickle cleanly
Scale a pickle recipe without changing its proportions
Store pepper sauces and oil-based sauces safely

blocks.text: Pickling preserves food with acid. In a vinegar pickle you add the acid yourself. WHO explains that botulism bacteria **will not grow in acidic conditions below pH 4.6**, so enough acid, spread evenly through every piece, is the safety line. Onions, cucumbers, carrots, garden eggs and peppers all pickle well and sell well beside suya, rice and small chops.

blocks.name: cucumber
blocks.caption: Crisp vegetables like cucumber, onion and carrot become pickles when vinegar makes them acidic.

blocks.text: The three pickling rules
The US National Center for Home Food Preservation, a widely used university reference for home preserving, gives three rules that matter most:

items: **Use vinegar of 5% acidity.** Check the label. White distilled vinegar of 5% acidity is the standard. Do not use vinegar of unknown strength.

**Do not change the proportions** of vinegar, water and vegetables in a tested recipe. Adding extra water or more vegetables weakens the acid. The guide states there must be a minimum, even level of acid throughout the product to prevent botulinum bacteria.
**Use pickling or canning salt** if the recipe asks for salt. The anti-caking additives in some table salts make the brine cloudy.

blocks.text: Preparing vegetables for pickling

items: Choose firm, fresh vegetables with no soft spots. Pickling will not firm up a limp cucumber or rescue a bruised onion.
Wash them well in safe water, scrubbing off soil, and trim away the flower end of cucumbers, which can soften pickles.
Cut pieces to an even size so the vinegar reaches the centre of every piece at the same rate.
Pack vegetables firmly but not crushed, so the liquid can flow around every piece and cover the top completely.
Wear gloves when cutting hot peppers such as scotch bonnet (ata rodo), and keep your hands away from your eyes.

blocks.text: Sterilising jars

items: Wash jars and lids in hot soapy water and rinse well.
Place the jars in a large pot, cover them fully with water and boil for 10 minutes.
Lift them out with clean tongs, drain upside down on a clean cloth, and fill while still hot.
Do not dry the inside with a towel; let them air-dry from their own heat.

blocks.text: Refrigerator pickles and shelf pickles

A **refrigerator pickle** is made by pouring a hot vinegar mixture over prepared vegetables in clean jars, cooling, and keeping the jars in the fridge. It is quick and suits small batches, but it is not shelf-stable. A **shelf pickle** is processed after filling in a boiling-water bath for a set time, following a tested recipe exactly. If you have not done that, treat your pickle as a fridge product and label it **Keep refrigerated**.

blocks.title: Safe acid pickle versus risky oil pack
items: Safer: vinegar pickle
Risky: vegetables under oil
blocks.caption: Acid protects the food; oil only shuts out air.
left: Fridge unless processed by tested method
right: Botulism risk with no warning signs

blocks.title: Worked example: tripling a fridge pickle without breaking it
blocks.context: For example, Ese sells pickled onion and carrot beside her husband's suya spot in Benin City. Her recipe card for 1 kg of vegetables uses 600 ml of 5% vinegar, 400 ml of water and 20 g of pickling salt. She wants three times as much for a weekend.
steps: Vegetables: 3 × 1 kg = 3 kg.
Vinegar: 3 × 600 ml = 1,800 ml. Water: 3 × 400 ml = 1,200 ml. Salt: 3 × 20 g = 60 g.
Check the balance: vinegar is 600 ÷ (600 + 400) = 60% of the liquid in the small batch, and 1,800 ÷ (1,800 + 1,200) = 60% in the big batch. The acid strength is unchanged.
Her sister suggests adding an extra litre of water to stretch it. Ese refuses: the vinegar share would fall to 1,800 ÷ 4,000 = 45%, weaker than the recipe.
She packs the vegetables into hot sterilised jars, covers them fully with the hot liquid, cools them and keeps them in the fridge.
blocks.result: Every jar has exactly the same acid level as the recipe, and her jars are clearly labelled Keep refrigerated.

blocks.text: Pepper sauces

Two kinds of pepper sauce are common. A **vinegar pepper sauce** is blended pepper, onion and spices cooked with vinegar to a tested recipe, poured hot into hot sterilised jars and refrigerated after opening. A **fried oil pepper sauce** such as ata din din is a cooked stew in oil. Treat it as cooked food: cool it quickly, keep it covered in the fridge, use a clean dry spoon, and use it within a few days. Raw blended pepper with onion or garlic, kept under oil at room temperature, is the dangerous one.

blocks.title: Scoop, do not dip
blocks.text: Never dip a used spoon, bread or suya into a jar of sauce or pickles. Saliva and food crumbs carry microbes into the jar. Pour or scoop out what you need with a clean spoon.

takeaways: Enough acid, evenly spread, is what makes a pickle safe.
Use 5% vinegar and never change the vinegar, water and vegetable proportions.
Sterilise jars by boiling them fully covered for 10 minutes and fill them hot.
Unless processed by a tested method, keep pickles and sauces in the fridge.
Raw garlic, onion or pepper under oil at room temperature is a botulism risk.

activity.title: Make a small refrigerator pickle
steps: Choose a tested refrigerator pickle recipe and copy its exact proportions into your notebook.
Check your vinegar label for 5% acidity and photograph it.
Sterilise two jars and make one batch, keeping the proportions exactly.
Label the jars with the product name, date and Keep refrigerated, and store them in the fridge.
activity.evidence: Photos of the vinegar label, the filled jars and their labels, plus your recipe card with quantities.

lessons.title: Jam and fruit spreads: pectin, sugar and sealing
objectives: Explain how pectin, acid and sugar work together to set and preserve jam
Make a jam that sets, using the cold saucer test
Fill and store jars safely, and know when a jar must be thrown away
Cost a jam batch and work out the cost per jar

blocks.text: Jam turns a glut of pineapple, guava, mango or oranges into a product that keeps for months unopened. Three things make it work. **Pectin**, a natural setting substance in fruit, forms a soft gel. **Acid**, from the fruit or added lemon juice, helps the pectin set. **Sugar** ties up the water in the fruit so moulds and bacteria cannot use it, and helps the gel form. If you cut the sugar a lot, the jam no longer keeps at room temperature.

blocks.name: pineapple
blocks.caption: Pineapple is plentiful and tasty but low in pectin, so it is often mixed with guava or citrus.

blocks.text: Choosing fruit

head: Fruit
Natural pectin
Tip
rows: Guava

Orange, lime, lemon (peel and pith)
High
Use for marmalade, or add a little to low-pectin fruit

blocks.text: Making jam step by step

items: Wash, peel and chop the fruit, removing bruised parts, and **weigh** it.
Put a few small saucers in the freezer or the coldest part of the fridge for testing.
Cook the fruit with a little water until soft. Add lemon juice if the fruit is low in acid or pectin.
Add the sugar your recipe gives. Many traditional recipes use roughly equal weights of prepared fruit and sugar. Stir over low heat until every crystal dissolves.
Turn up the heat and boil hard, stirring often so it does not burn.
Test for set: drop a little jam on a cold saucer, wait a minute, then push it with your finger. If the surface wrinkles, it is ready. If it runs, boil a few minutes more and test again.
Pour the hot jam into hot sterilised jars, leaving a small space at the top, wipe the rims with a clean cloth, close at once and label.

blocks.title: Making a jam that sets and keeps
items: Prepare and weigh fruit
Cook fruit soft
Dissolve sugar, boil hard
Cold saucer wrinkle test
Hot-fill sterilised jars
blocks.caption: Weighing and the saucer test make each batch set the same way.

blocks.title: Boiling jam burns
blocks.text: Boiling sugar mixture is much hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Use a deep heavy pot filled no more than half full, a long wooden spoon, and keep children away from the stove. Fill jars on a board, not by holding them in your hand.

blocks.title: Worked example: cost per jar of pineapple and orange jam
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Ilorin makes jam to sell at her church bazaar. She uses 4 pineapples at about ₦1,500 each, which give 2 kg of prepared fruit, plus 2 kg of sugar at about ₦1,800 per kg, ₦500 of oranges and lemons, 14 jars at about ₦400 each and labels at about ₦50 each (approximate prices).
steps: She fills 14 jars of 250 g, so the batch gives 14 × 250 g = 3,500 g of jam.
Cost per jar: ₦16,400 ÷ 14 = about ₦1,171.
blocks.result: Grace knows each jar costs about ₦1,171 before gas and her time, and she can see that jars and labels are over a third of her cost: ₦6,300 of ₦16,400.

head: Problem
Likely cause

blocks.text: Storing jam

items: Store unopened jars in a cool, dark cupboard.
After opening, keep the jar covered in the fridge and always use a clean, dry spoon.
Low-sugar or reduced-sugar fruit spreads must be kept in the fridge and used quickly.
If you see mould on jam, throw away the whole jar. Do not scrape off the top and eat the rest: mould threads can grow well below the surface you can see.
Also throw away jars with bulging lids, a fizzy or alcoholic smell, or leaks.

takeaways: Pectin, acid and sugar together make jam set and keep.
Mix low-pectin fruit like pineapple with guava or citrus, or add lemon juice.
The cold saucer wrinkle test tells you when jam is ready.
Hot-fill hot sterilised jars and refrigerate after opening.
Mould on jam means the whole jar goes in the bin.

activity.title: Make one small batch of jam
steps: Weigh 1 kg of prepared fruit and record whether it is high or low in pectin.
Make the jam using a recipe, recording the weights of fruit and sugar and the cooking time.
Use the cold saucer test and note how many tests it took.
Fill sterilised jars, label them, and calculate the cost per jar.
Open one jar after a week and check set, taste and appearance.
