quiz.q: Ese's pickle recipe uses 600 ml vinegar and 400 ml water for 1 kg of vegetables. How much vinegar does she need for 2.5 kg?
quiz.explain: 2.5 × 600 ml = 1,500 ml, keeping the same proportion as the recipe.

quiz.q: Why must you never add extra water to a vinegar pickle recipe?
options: It makes the jar too heavy
It weakens the acid that keeps botulism bacteria from growing
quiz.explain: The safety of a pickle depends on enough acid throughout. Extra water dilutes it.

quiz.q: Tolu's ogi smells clean and sour but has pink patches on the surface. What should she do?
options: Scrape off the pink part and sell the rest
quiz.explain: Pink, black, green or orange patches show unwanted microbes. A spoiled ferment should be discarded.

quiz.q: Grace's jam drops on a cold saucer and runs when pushed. What next?
options: Boil it a few minutes more and test again
Put the pot in the fridge
quiz.explain: If the surface does not wrinkle, the jam has not set. Boil a little longer and test again.

quiz.q: Which fruit most needs help from guava, citrus or bought pectin to set?
quiz.explain: Pineapple is low in pectin, so it is mixed with high-pectin fruit or given added pectin.

quiz.q: Ese's sister wants to add 1 litre of water to 1,800 ml vinegar and 1,200 ml water. What share of the liquid would be vinegar?

modules.title: Cold Storage, Shop Storage and Selling
modules.overview: Protect food in the fridge and freezer through power cuts, run a dry store and shop shelf that loses nothing to dates or pests, and pack, label and price your preserved products honestly.

lessons.title: Fridge and freezer: the cold chain at home when power is unreliable
objectives: Set up and check a fridge and freezer so food stays at safe temperatures
Cool, portion, freeze and thaw food the safe way
Use the 4-hour, 24-hour and 48-hour guide to decide what to keep after a power cut
Plan generator or grid hours and freezer packing to protect food

blocks.text: The **cold chain** is the unbroken line of cold that keeps perishable food safe from the moment it is caught, slaughtered or cooked until it is eaten. At home, the weak links are a fridge that is too warm, cooked food left out too long, and power cuts. This lesson shows you how to protect each link.

blocks.name: thermometer
blocks.caption: A cheap fridge thermometer tells you whether your fridge is really cold enough.

blocks.text: Know your temperatures

items: **Fridge:** WHO advises refrigerating cooked and perishable food promptly, preferably **below 5°C**. Buy a fridge thermometer and check it in the morning before anyone opens the door.
**Freezer:** a freezer should keep food frozen rock hard. **-18°C** is the temperature commonly recommended for home freezers.
**Room temperature:** WHO advises not leaving cooked food at room temperature for more than **2 hours**.

blocks.text: Setting up the fridge

items: Keep ready-to-eat and cooked food on the upper shelves, in covered containers.
Keep raw meat, chicken and fish on the lowest shelf, in a covered bowl or tray, so juices cannot drip onto other food. This follows the WHO key: separate raw and cooked.
Do not overpack. Cold air must move around the food.
Clean spills at once and wipe the shelves weekly.

blocks.text: Cooling, freezing and thawing

items: **Cool cooked food fast.** Divide a big pot of stew or soup into shallow containers so it cools quickly, and get it into the fridge or freezer within 2 hours of cooking.
**Freeze in meal-sized portions.** Flat bags freeze and thaw faster than deep tubs, and you only take out what you need.
**Label everything** with the food name and the date. Frozen food all looks alike after a month.
**Blanch vegetables** such as ugwu or green beans briefly in boiling water and cool them before freezing, so they keep their colour.
**Thaw safely.** WHO advises against thawing frozen food at room temperature. Move it to the fridge the night before, or thaw it in the microwave and cook it at once.
**Reheat thoroughly.** Bring soups and stews back to a full boil before serving.

blocks.text: When the power goes off

FoodSafety.gov, the US government food safety site, gives clear guidance for power cuts. Keep the doors closed as much as possible. A closed fridge keeps food safe for up to about **4 hours**. A **full** freezer holds its temperature for about **48 hours**, and a **half-full** freezer for about **24 hours**, if the door stays closed. Perishable food that has been at **4°C or above for more than 2 hours** should be thrown away. Frozen food can be refrozen if it **still contains ice crystals** or is at 4°C or below, though the quality may drop.

blocks.title: How long cold lasts in a power cut
items: Power goes off
Fridge: about 4 hours
Half-full freezer: about 24 hours
Full freezer: about 48 hours
blocks.caption: Keeping doors closed and freezers full stretches the time your food stays safe.

blocks.title: Fill empty freezer space
blocks.text: A full freezer stays cold longer. Fill empty spaces with clean bottles of water. Once frozen, they act like ice blocks during an outage, and you can move a few into the fridge or a cool box to keep it cold.

blocks.title: Worked example: deciding after an overnight outage
blocks.context: For example, Kemi in Port Harcourt loses power at 8 pm. It returns at 2 pm the next day. Her fridge has cooked stew, fresh fish and a carton of fruit juice. Her freezer is about half full of chicken and blended pepper. Nobody opened either door.
steps: Length of the outage: from 8 pm to midnight is 4 hours, and from midnight to 2 pm is 14 hours, so 4 + 14 = 18 hours.
Fridge: 18 hours is far beyond the 4-hour guide, and her thermometer reads 12°C. The cooked stew and fresh fish are perishable and have been above 4°C for many hours, so she throws them away.
Freezer: 18 hours is less than the 24-hour guide for a half-full freezer. She checks the chicken and finds it still hard with ice crystals, so it can be refrozen.
The blended pepper has ice crystals too, so it goes back in.
Next time she plans to fill the empty half of the freezer with water bottles and to cook the fish on the day she buys it.
blocks.result: Kemi keeps the frozen food, discards the risky fridge food without tasting it, and changes her habits to stretch future outages.

blocks.text: Planning your power hours

If you rely on a generator or a few grid hours, run the freezer during the longest block you can and keep the door shut at other times. Open the fridge as rarely as possible: decide what you need, open, take it, close. Before a known long outage, freeze bottles of water, move tomorrow's food to the fridge, and cook fresh fish or meat rather than holding it raw.

takeaways: Keep the fridge below 5°C and check it with a thermometer.
Cool cooked food fast in shallow containers and refrigerate it within 2 hours.
Thaw in the fridge or microwave, never on the counter.
Power cut guide: fridge about 4 hours, half-full freezer about 24, full freezer about 48, doors closed.
Refreeze only food that still has ice crystals or is at 4°C or below.

activity.title: Cold chain check at home
steps: Put a thermometer in your fridge and record the morning temperature for five days.
Rearrange the fridge so raw food is covered on the bottom shelf and cooked food is above.
Label and date every item in your freezer, and fill empty space with water bottles.
Write a one-page outage plan for your household, using the 4, 24 and 48 hour guide.
activity.evidence: Five days of temperature readings, a photo of the rearranged fridge, and your written outage plan.

lessons.title: Dry storage and stock rotation in a home store or provisions shop
objectives: Set up a dry store that keeps out damp, heat, pests and chemicals
Rotate stock using first in first out and first expired first out
Explain the difference between best before and use by dates
Calculate how many weeks of stock you hold and spot overstock before it expires

blocks.text: Most food in a Nigerian home or provisions shop never sees a fridge: rice, beans, garri, flour, pasta, tins, oil, sugar, noodles, dried fish, crayfish and your own dried and bottled products. They are safe for a long time only if the store is clean, dry, cool and organised. A badly kept store loses money quietly, one expired tin and one weevil-filled bag at a time.

blocks.name: groceries
blocks.alt: A woman carrying a bag of groceries
blocks.caption: Good storage protects every item a household or shop buys, from rice to tinned tomatoes.

blocks.text: Rules for a good dry store

items: **Off the floor, away from the wall.** Keep bags and cartons on pallets, shelves or planks so air flows underneath and you can see and clean behind them.
**Cool and shaded.** Keep oils, groundnuts, chocolate and bottled products away from sunny windows, zinc roofs and the cooking area. Heat speeds rancidity and spoilage.
**Dry.** Keep away from leaking roofs, sinks and damp walls. Damp brings mould to garri, flour and grains.
**Closed containers.** Once a big bag of rice, beans or garri is opened, move it into clean containers with tight lids, so insects and rats cannot reach it.
**Chemicals apart.** Store kerosene, insecticides, detergents and bleach on a separate shelf, below and away from food, never in old food or drink bottles.
**Pest watch.** Look for droppings, gnawed bags, webbing, holes in grains and live insects. Keep the floor swept and spills cleaned the same day.

blocks.text: If you find insects in one bag of beans or rice, move that bag away from the rest at once, check the bags around it, and clean the shelf before restocking. Use sealed traps or a professional pest service rather than scattering rat poison or spraying insecticide near open food, and keep any poison locked away from food, children and animals.
Best before and use by

head: Date mark
What it means
What to do
rows: Use by / expiry date
Safety date for perishable foods
Do not sell or eat after this date. WHO's Five Keys advise not using food beyond its expiry date
Best before
Quality date; the food is at its best until then if stored as directed
Do not sell past this date; check quality and storage instructions
Date of manufacture / production
When the food was made
Use it with the shelf life to work out the expiry

blocks.title: Never change a date
blocks.text: Covering, scratching out or reprinting a date on food is dishonest and puts customers at risk. If stock is close to its date, sell it sooner at a fair price or remove it, never relabel it.
FIFO and FEFO

**FIFO** means **first in, first out**: the stock you received first is sold or used first. **FEFO** means **first expired, first out**: the item with the earliest date goes first, even if it arrived later. FEFO is safer for anything with a date. In practice: put new stock at the **back** of the shelf and bring older or earlier-dated stock to the **front**.

blocks.title: Stock rotation cycle
items: Receive and check dates
New stock behind old
Earliest date sells first
Weekly date check
Reorder by real sales
blocks.caption: Each week the cycle catches near-date stock before it becomes a loss.

items: When stock arrives, check every carton: dates, dents, swelling, tears, leaks, damp and pests. Refuse damaged items.
Write the delivery date on the carton with a marker.
Place new stock behind older stock, earliest expiry at the front.
Once a week, check dates on every shelf and list anything due within a month.
Remove any bulging, leaking, rusted or badly dented tins, and any packs with mould or insects.

blocks.title: Worked example: weeks of stock and an overstock warning
blocks.context: For example, Ada runs a provisions shop in Owerri. On her weekly check she finds 7 packs of biscuits past their best-before date, priced at about ₦300 each, and 48 packs of spaghetti whose best-before date is 3 weeks away. She sells about 12 packs of spaghetti a week.
steps: Biscuits lost: 7 × ₦300 = ₦2,100 of stock she can no longer sell.
Spaghetti cover: 48 ÷ 12 = 4 weeks of stock, but only 3 weeks are left before the date.
At her normal speed she will sell 3 × 12 = 36 packs in time, leaving 48 − 36 = 12 packs at risk.
She moves the spaghetti to the front counter, offers it in a bundle with tomato paste, and orders no more spaghetti until the shelf is down to one week of stock.
She also cuts her biscuit order, since that line sells slower than she thought.
blocks.result: Ada stops a likely loss on 12 packs of spaghetti and learns to order by weekly sales, not by the size of the supplier's discount.

blocks.title: Mouldy groundnuts, maize and garri
blocks.text: Sort groundnuts and maize before storing and selling, removing mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured ones. WHO notes that staples such as maize and groundnuts can carry aflatoxins, mould poisons. Do not sell or eat mouldy portions.

takeaways: Keep stock off the floor, away from walls, cool, dry and in closed containers.
Store chemicals apart from food and never in food bottles.
Use FEFO: earliest date at the front, new stock at the back.
Never sell food past its date or change a date.
Weeks of stock = stock on hand ÷ weekly sales; compare it with the time left before the date.

activity.title: Rotate and audit one shelf
steps: Choose one shelf or cupboard and take everything out.
Clean the shelf, then check each item's date and condition, removing damaged or expired items.
Put items back with the earliest dates at the front.
For three items, count the stock, estimate weekly sales and calculate weeks of stock.
Write down anything due within a month and your plan to use or sell it.
activity.evidence: Before and after photos of the shelf and a short audit sheet with dates, weeks of stock and actions.

lessons.title: Packing, labelling and pricing preserved food to sell
objectives: Choose packaging that protects each type of preserved food
Write an honest label with the information a buyer needs
Set a best-before date from your own storage test
Price a preserved product from its full cost, including your time

blocks.text: Once you can preserve food reliably, selling the surplus is a natural next step: dried tomato flakes, smoked fish, pickles, jam or ogi to neighbours, your church, your shop or WhatsApp customers. Selling adds three new duties: packaging that keeps the food as good as the day you made it, a label that tells the truth, and a price that covers every cost.

blocks.name: for-sale
blocks.alt: A woman putting up a for sale sign
blocks.caption: Selling preserved food well starts with honest packing, labelling and pricing.

blocks.text: Packaging by product

head: Product
Good packaging
Why
rows: Dried tomato, vegetables, mango
Thick food-grade zip or heat-sealed bags, or glass jars
Keeps out damp air and insects
Hard-smoked fish
Paper or carton inside, loosely closed; sealed plastic only when fully cool and dry
Fish must not sweat; trapped damp grows mould
Pickles and sauces
Sterilised glass jars with good lids
Acid attacks some metals; glass is easy to sterilise
Jam
Sterilised glass jars, filled hot
Hot-filling and a clean seal protect the jam
Ogi
Clean food bags or leaves, kept cool, sold within days
It keeps only a short time

blocks.text: What your label should say

items: Product name that says what it is, for example Sun-dried tomato flakes.
Ingredients, largest amount first.
Net weight or volume.
Date made and best-before date.
Storage instructions, for example Keep in a cool dry place, or Refrigerate after opening, or Keep refrigerated.
Your business name and phone number, so customers can reach you.

blocks.text: If you plan to sell packaged food beyond your immediate neighbours, for example through supermarkets, other shops or across states, it will need registration with NAFDAC, the agency that regulates packaged food in Nigeria. Check NAFDAC's guidance for small businesses before you scale up.
Setting an honest best-before date

items: Keep back at least three packs from a batch, stored exactly as a customer would store them.
Open and check one every week or two: look, smell, texture and taste of a pack with no warning signs.
Write down the week the quality first drops (softening, darkening, loss of crunch, any mould).
Set your best-before date well inside that time, for example at around half to two-thirds of the time it stayed good.
Repeat the test whenever you change the recipe, the packaging or the supplier.

blocks.title: What your price must cover
items: Ingredients
Packaging and labels
Fuel and transport
Your labour
Profit
blocks.caption: Price from the bottom up: every layer must be paid before the top layer is profit.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a 100 g pack of tomato flakes
blocks.context: For example, Funmi from Module 2 now dries 20 kg of tomatoes a month at about ₦1,200 per kg. She knows her drying ratio is 10, so she expects 2 kg of flakes. Bags cost about ₦100 each, labels about ₦50, transport to market about ₦1,500, and she values her 6 hours of work at ₦500 an hour (approximate figures).
steps: Transport ₦1,500. Labour 6 × ₦500 = ₦3,000.
She adds 40%: ₦1,575 × 1.4 = ₦2,205, and rounds to ₦2,250 a pack, a profit of ₦2,250 − ₦1,575 = ₦675 per pack, or 20 × ₦675 = ₦13,500 a month.
blocks.result: Funmi has a price that pays for her time as well as her tomatoes. If buyers in her area will only pay much less, she knows it is her costs, not her guesswork, that need to change.

blocks.title: Take orders before you produce
blocks.text: Short-life products such as ogi, soft-smoked fish and fridge pickles are safest and most profitable when you take orders by WhatsApp first and produce only what is ordered. Long-life products such as well-dried foods and jam can be made ahead in planned batches.
Keeping products safe at the point of sale

items: Display jars and packs in the shade, never on a hot bench in the sun or on top of a fridge or generator.
Keep fridge products (fridge pickles, soft-smoked fish, ogi) in a cool box with frozen water bottles when you take them to market, and do not display them warm for hours.
Do not open packs for tasting from stock you will sell. Make a separate tasting jar and serve with clean spoons.
When a customer pays by transfer to Opay, Moniepoint or a bank, confirm the money has arrived in your app before handing over goods.

blocks.text: Keep a simple record for every batch: date, quantities in, quantities out, costs, the batch code on the labels, and any customer comments. If a customer reports a problem, the record tells you which jars or packs came from the same batch so you can check them quickly.

takeaways: Match packaging to the product: airtight for dried food, breathable for hard-smoked fish, sterilised glass for pickles and jam.
A label needs the name, ingredients, net weight, dates, storage instructions and your contact.
Set best-before dates from your own storage test, well inside the time quality held.
Price from full cost, including packaging, transport and your labour.
Packaged food sold widely needs NAFDAC registration.

activity.title: Price and label one product
steps: Choose one preserved product you have made in this course.
List every cost for one batch, including packaging, transport and your time.
Calculate cost per pack and choose a selling price.
Design a label with all six items from this lesson.
Keep three packs back and start your best-before storage test.
activity.evidence: A costing sheet, a photo of your labelled product, and the start of your storage test log.

quiz.q: Power goes off at 10 pm and returns at 6 am the next day. How long was the outage?
quiz.explain: From 10 pm to midnight is 2 hours, and from midnight to 6 am is 6 hours: 2 + 6 = 8 hours.

quiz.q: After that 8-hour outage, Kemi's fridge thermometer reads 11°C. What should she do with leftover cooked stew in the fridge?
quiz.explain: The stew has been above 4°C for more than 2 hours, beyond the 4-hour fridge guide, so it should be discarded.

quiz.q: A half-full freezer stayed shut during a 20-hour outage. The chicken still has ice crystals. What is correct?
options: Leave it out to finish thawing
quiz.explain: Food that still contains ice crystals can be refrozen, and 20 hours is within the 24-hour half-full freezer guide.

quiz.q: Ada has 60 tins of tomato paste and sells 15 a week. The best-before date is 3 weeks away. How many tins are at risk?
quiz.explain: In 3 weeks she sells 3 × 15 = 45 tins, leaving 60 − 45 = 15 at risk.

quiz.q: Which is the safest way to thaw frozen fish?
options: In the fridge the night before
In the sun in a bowl
quiz.explain: WHO advises against thawing at room temperature. Thaw in the fridge, or in the microwave and cook at once.

quiz.q: A product's full cost is ₦1,200 per pack. Using a 40% markup, what is the price?
Where should a new delivery of tinned tomato be placed on the shelf?
options: Behind older stock with earlier dates
On the floor near the door
quiz.explain: FEFO: earliest dates at the front, new stock behind, and chemicals kept away from food.

finalQuiz.q: Which pair of conditions does WHO say botulism bacteria need to grow?
options: Plenty of air and high acid
No oxygen and low acid (pH 4.6 or above)
finalQuiz.explain: WHO explains the bacterium grows only without oxygen and will not grow below pH 4.6.

finalQuiz.q: Bisi bought 40 tomatoes for ₦12,000 and 6 are bruised. What are the bruised tomatoes worth?
Which WHO key is broken when raw chicken is stored above cooked rice in the fridge?
finalQuiz.explain: Raw meat should be stored below and apart from cooked food so juices cannot drip onto it.

finalQuiz.q: Funmi's dried mango feels dry, but drops of water appear in her conditioning jar. Next step?
finalQuiz.explain: Moisture during conditioning means some pieces still hold water; dry more before packing.

finalQuiz.q: Rukayat smokes 12 kg of fresh fish and gets 4.2 kg. What is her yield?
Lightly salted fish that has not been dried should be:
options: Sealed in a jar at room temperature
Refrigerated and cooked soon, or fully dried or smoked
Left in the sun without a net
finalQuiz.explain: Light salting alone does not preserve fish; it needs drying, smoking or the fridge.

finalQuiz.q: Ogi kept at home should be stored:
options: Open to the air to keep it fresh
Under a layer of safe water changed daily, covered
In a sealed tin for months
finalQuiz.explain: A layer of safe water changed daily, in a covered container, keeps ogi fresh for a few days.

finalQuiz.q: A pickle recipe uses 500 ml vinegar and 500 ml water. A cook wants to use 700 ml water with the same vinegar. Why is this unsafe?
options: It makes the pickle too salty
It lowers the vinegar share and weakens the acid
It is safe if refrigerated forever
finalQuiz.explain: The vinegar share drops from 50% to about 42%, weakening the acid that protects against botulism.

finalQuiz.q: You find a small patch of mould on top of an unopened jar of jam. What should you do?
options: Scrape it off and eat the rest
finalQuiz.explain: Mould threads grow below the visible surface. Discard the whole jar.

finalQuiz.q: A full freezer that stays closed during a power cut holds safe temperatures for about:
finalQuiz.explain: FoodSafety.gov gives about 48 hours for a full freezer and about 24 hours for a half-full one.

finalQuiz.q: Ada has 36 tins and sells 9 a week, with 3 weeks until the best-before date. What should she do?
options: Nothing, all will sell in time
Promote 9 tins that will not sell in time
finalQuiz.explain: 3 × 9 = 27 tins sell in time, leaving 36 − 27 = 9 at risk, so she should sell them sooner.

finalQuiz.q: A batch costs ₦18,000 for 12 packs. With a 40% markup, what is the price per pack?

capstone.title: Household or shop preservation plan with two finished products
capstone.brief: Produce two different preserved products using two different methods from this course, test their keeping quality, and present a one-page preservation and storage plan for your household or shop, including a power-cut plan, FEFO shelf audit, labels and a costed price for each product.
steps: Choose two foods your household or shop often wastes and select a different method for each, explaining why.
Make one batch of each, recording weights, method, dates and costs on a batch record sheet.
Apply the safety checks: Five Keys, acid or dryness checks, and no low-acid food under oil or sealed at room temperature.
Pack and label both products with all six label items, and start a storage test with three packs of each.
Audit one shelf or cupboard using FEFO, and write your household fridge and freezer power-cut plan.
Cost and price each product, and share samples with at least three people for feedback.
evidence: Batch record sheets for both products with weights and yields
Photos of each stage and the labelled finished products
Safety checklist completed for each product
Storage test log covering at least four weeks
FEFO shelf audit sheet and power-cut plan
Costing sheets with cost per pack and selling price
